field_sets.expect: A Native American manifesto challenges social scientists and institutions; its particular arguments await primary chapter review.
field_sets.value: In Custer Died for Your Sins: An Indian Manifesto (1969), Deloria condemns the damage done by government and private interventions in Native life and criticizes anthropology’s treatment of living Native communities as objects of detached research. Robert L. Bennett welcomed the book’s intervention in 1970 but judged its proposed remedies insufficiently developed. Reviewing the essay collection Indians and Anthropologists (1997) in 1999, Donald D. Stull wrote that the book had shaken cultural anthropology, dividing the discipline’s history into before and after Deloria.
Custer Died for Your Sins: An Indian Manifesto (1969).

field_sets.expect: Métis scholar’s critique of Canadian colonialism joins historical interpretation and Marxist politics. The institutional biography dates his doctorate and university appointment to 1966; detailed book arguments remain outside this description-level inclusion.
field_sets.value: Prison of Grass: Canada from a Native Point of View (1975) combines autobiography and historical interpretation to explain Canadian colonialism through its racist and capitalist structures and its effects on Indigenous self-understanding. Adams challenges official historical accounts and calls for decolonization through revolutionary struggle. Reviewing the revised edition in 1992, Barnett Richling noted that the book had first drawn lukewarm reviews for its historical scholarship and generalizations, but judged it an early and valuable commentary on the connections between historiography and colonial context; he regretted that the revision added practically nothing to its 1970s argument.

field_sets.expect: Māori historical interpretation and political struggle in Aotearoa New Zealand; one regionally situated contribution.
field_sets.value: Ka Whawhai Tonu Mātou: Struggle Without End (1990) recasts Aotearoa New Zealand’s history around Māori resistance to colonial domination and the continuing pursuit of autonomy. Walker connects historical interpretation to struggles for justice, equality and self-determination. Paul Moon’s 1996 review recognized the book as a landmark general history that widened Māori historical analysis, while questioning its selective framing and some of its generalizations.

field_sets.expect: Natick land loss and strategic kinship/institutional adaptation challenge an uncomplicated disappearance narrative.
field_sets.value: In Dispossession by Degrees: Indian Land and Identity in Natick, Massachusetts, 1650–1790 (1997), O’Brien shows how colonial land loss produced an appearance of Indigenous disappearance despite continuing resistance and strategic use of English institutions. Firsting and Lasting: Writing Indians out of Existence in New England (2010) argues that nineteenth-century local histories claimed modernity for settlers while denying it to Indigenous peoples, helping discredit their land and political rights. Hilary E. Wyss’s 2011 review praised the latter book’s persuasive explanation of how these recurring historical patterns continue to shape the present.
